papers.what_it_is: CompVQC, an ADMM-based, compilation-aware pruning and quantization framework that shortens the transpiled circuits of variational quantum circuits, tested on Qiskit Aer and IBM processors.

assertions.value: The authors report that CompVQC reduced the circuit depth of quantum neural networks with an accuracy drop under 1%, on the MNIST and Fashion-MNIST datasets.
quotes: with a negligible accuracy drop (<1%), which outperforms other competitors.
Results on the MNIST and Fashion-MNIST dataset demonstrate that CompVQC can outperform vanilla VQC with significant circuit length reduction with less than 1% accuracy degradation.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on small tasks (2 to 4 classes, downsampled images).
assertions.reader_inference: The depth reduction factor is printed with a symbol that pdftotext drops, so it is left out of the value; Table 2 gives it per method.

assertions.value: The authors report that on two synthetic datasets run on IBM Quantum processors, CompVQC gave up to 20% accuracy improvement over vanilla VQC, and that vanilla VQC lost 15% and 10% accuracy on the two datasets when deployed to the real processors.
quotes: Compared with Vanilla VQC, CompVQC achieves upto 20% accuracy improvement.
the Vanilla VQC has a 15% and 10% accuracy drop on two datasets respectively, after deploying the VQC to the real quantum processors
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical hardware result from one study on synthetic datasets with 4 and 16 features.
assertions.reader_inference: The hardware test uses synthetic data only, so it does not show the same gain on MNIST-type tasks.

assertions.value: The authors state that they evaluate CompVQC on 2 common classification datasets (MNIST and Fashion MNIST) and one synthetic dataset, and that for MNIST they extract 2 classes, the digits 3 and 6.
quotes: We evaluate CompVQC on 2 common classification datasets (MNIST [24] and Fashion MNIST [36]) and one synthetic dataset.
For MNIST, we extract 2 classes (i.e., digits 3 and 6), denoted as
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup, Section 4.1, p.6.
assertions.reader_inference: Binary and few-class tasks on small images limit how far the depth and accuracy figures transfer.

assertions.value: The authors report that when the compression ratio reaches 0.8, the metric of CompVQC decreases, which they attribute mainly to a decrease in accuracy.
quotes: When the compression ratio reaches 0.8, we observe a decrease of metrics on CompVQC, this is mainly because the accuracy is decreased.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical ablation result from one study, one dataset (Fashion-MNIST-2).
assertions.reader_inference: Compression has a limit past which accuracy loss outweighs depth gain.

papers.title_in_file: Battle Against Fluctuating Quantum Noise: Compression-Aided Framework to Enable Robust Quantum Neural Network
papers.what_it_is: QuCAD, a noise-aware compression framework with an offline model repository that adapts a trained quantum neural network to fluctuating qubit noise, tested by emulation and on ibm-jakarta.

assertions.value: The authors report that in emulation on an earthquake detection dataset, QuCAD achieved 14.91% accuracy gain on average over 146 days compared with a noise-aware training approach.
quotes: Emulation results on an earthquake detection dataset show that QuCAD can achieve 14.91% accuracy gain on average in 146 days over a noise-aware training approach.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical emulation result from one study using recorded calibration data.

assertions.value: The authors report that on the 7-qubit IBM processor ibm-jakarta, QuCAD outperformed the two competitors by 13.7% and 12.52% on average on the earthquake detection dataset.
assertions.anchor: Abstract p.1 and Section IV, evaluation on real quantum computers (Fig. 8)
quotes: For the execution on a 7-qubit IBM quantum processor, ibm-jakarta, QuCAD can consistently achieve 12.52% accuracy gain on earthquake detection.
QuCAD can consistently outperform the two competitors by 13.7% and 12.52% on average.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical hardware result from one study on one dataset and one device.
assertions.reader_inference: The text gives 12.52% as the gain in the abstract and 13.7% and 12.52% as the gains over the two competitors; the paper does not name which competitor each figure belongs to in these sentences.

assertions.value: The authors report that a noise-aware trained model had accuracy over 80% from day 1 to day 22, and that its accuracy decreased to 22% on day 24 when error rates increased.
quotes: over 80% from day 1 to day 22; however, when error rates increased on day 24, the accuracy decreased to 22%.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single empirical observation on one backend's recorded noise history.
assertions.reader_inference: This is the paper's motivating limitation of noise-aware training: it fails when noise drifts.

assertions.value: The authors state that the earthquake detection data is 1500 samples from FDSN, with features encoded to 4 qubits using the same VQC as the MNIST task.
quotes: We extract 1500 samples of the earthquake detection dataset from FDSN [26].
We encode features to 4 qubits and employ the same VQC as MNIST.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup in Section IV.
assertions.reader_inference: The models are 4-qubit circuits, so the robustness gains are shown only at that size.

papers.title_in_file: Experimental Quantum Generative Adversarial Networks for Image Generation
papers.what_it_is: A resource-efficient quantum GAN scheme (patch and batch variants) run on a superconducting processor to generate handwritten digit images and gray-scale bar images.

assertions.value: The authors state that they experimentally achieve, for the first time, the learning and generating of real-world hand-written digit images on a superconducting quantum processor, using up to 6 adjacent qubits of a 12-qubit device.
quotes: For the first time, we experimentally achieve the learning and generating of real-world hand-written digit images on a superconducting quantum processor.
the superconducting quantum processor has 12 transmon qubits on a 1D chain, and up to 6 adjacent qubits are chosen in the entire experiment.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical hardware demonstration from one study; priority claim is the authors' own.
assertions.reader_inference: Only digits 0 and 1 are generated, so the demonstration is small.

assertions.value: The authors report that on a gray-scale bar image dataset, two classical GANs requested more training parameters than the quantum patch GAN to reach similar FD scores, and that they did not search hyper-parameters for the quantum GAN while they did for the classical GANs.
quotes: The employed two classical GANs request more training parameters than the quantum patch GAN to achieve similar FD scores.
This result implies that quantum GAN has the potential advantage of reducing training parameters.
while we did not search for these hyper-parameters for quantum GAN.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on a synthetic dataset, five repeats per setting.
assertions.reader_inference: The authors word the finding as a potential advantage, not a demonstrated one. The comparison is on a tiny synthetic dataset.

assertions.value: The authors state that the experimental quantum GAN output similar quality images to the simulated quantum GAN, which they say suggests the proposal is insensitive to noise at their current noise levels and for this system size.
quotes: the experimental quantum GAN output similar quality images to the simulated quantum GAN, suggesting that our proposal is insensitive to noise at our current noise levels and for this system size.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical observation from one experiment, qualitative image comparison.
assertions.reader_inference: The qualifier 'for this system size' limits the claim to the small circuit used.

assertions.value: The authors state that it remains unknown whether the optimization of the minimax loss encounters barren plateaus, and name experimental exploration of trainability on large-scale datasets as a research direction.
quotes: It remains unknown whether the optimization of a minimax loss in Eqn. (1) encounters barren plateaus.
an intrigued research direction is experimentally exploring the trainability of quantum GANs on large-scale datasets.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own open limit in the Discussion, p.5.

papers.title_in_file: Information-theoretic bounds on quantum advantage in machine learning
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Sections I to VI (introduction, ML settings, average-case Theorem 1, worst-case Theorems 2 and 3, numerical experiments, conclusion). Appendices (proofs) not read.
papers.what_it_is: A learning-theory paper that bounds quantum advantage in predicting outcomes of physical experiments: no large advantage for average error, exponential advantage possible for worst-case error.

assertions.value: The paper proves that for any input distribution, a classical ML model can provide accurate predictions on average by accessing the process a number of times comparable to the optimal quantum ML model.
assertions.anchor: Abstract p.1; Theorem 1, Section III, p.3
quotes: We prove that for any input distribution D(x), a classical ML model can provide accurate predictions on average by accessing E a number of times comparable to the optimal quantum ML model.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 1, p.3 (proof sketch given; full proof in the appendices, which were not read).
assertions.reader_inference: The result counts runs of the physical process only. It is not a statement about runtime.

assertions.value: The paper proves that for predicting expectations of all Pauli observables in an n-qubit system, classical ML models face an exponential lower bound on the number of copies, while it presents a quantum ML model using only O(n) copies, an exponential gap.
assertions.anchor: Abstract p.1; Theorems 2 and 3, Section IV, p.4-5
quotes: In contrast, for achieving accurate prediction on all inputs, we prove that exponential quantum advantage is possible.
but we present a quantum ML model using only O(n) copies.
Theorem 3 establishes an exponential gap separating classical ML models from fully quantum ML models.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorems 2 and 3, Section IV, p.4-5 (full proofs in Appendix E, not read).
assertions.reader_inference: The quantum model needs coherent access to the state over several copies, so the advantage needs quantum memory.

assertions.value: The authors state that, for the comparison, they disregard the runtime of the classical or quantum ML models that generate predictions, and count only how many times the process must run during the learning phase; they note that a substantial quantum advantage in computational complexity is possible.
quotes: For the purpose of this comparison, we disregard the runtime of the classical or quantum ML models that generate the predictions;
a substantial quantum advantage in computational complexity is possible
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own scope in Section I, p.2.
assertions.reader_inference: The no-advantage result does not rule out a runtime advantage.

assertions.value: The authors report in numerical experiments that for mixed states there is an exponential separation in copies needed between classical and quantum ML, whereas for the class of product states the separation is much less pronounced.
quotes: However, for the class of product states, the separation is much less pronounced.
The separation between classical ML and quantum ML is marginal for product states.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result using best-known procedures on two state classes.
assertions.reader_inference: The exponential separation depends on the state class.

papers.title_in_file: Coreset selection can accelerate quantum machine learning models with provable generalization
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, related work, preliminaries, theorem statements (Theorems 1 and 2), numerical experiments (Sections 6.1 to 6.3), discussion. Appendix proofs not read.
papers.what_it_is: A method that selects a coreset (k-center) of the training data to speed up QNN and quantum kernel training, with generalization bounds and numerical simulations.

assertions.value: The authors state that they analyze the generalization error bounds of QNNs and quantum kernels trained on coresets, and that the bounds show comparable performance to training on the complete original dataset.
quotes: we analyze the generalization error bounds of QNNs and quantum kernels when trained on such coresets, unveiling the comparable performance with those training on the complete original dataset.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorems 1 and 2 (generalization bounds on coreset); proofs in Appendix A.1 and A.2, not read. The theorems carry Lipschitz-continuity assumptions.
assertions.reader_inference: The bounds are conditional on stated assumptions such as a Lipschitz continuous class-specific regression function.

assertions.value: The authors report in numerical simulation on synthetic data that, to reach the same test accuracy, the model needs only 250 coreset examples against 400 randomly sampled examples.
quotes: when achieving the same test accuracy, the model only needs 250 coreset examples while requiring 400 randomly sampled examples.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result from one study, five trials per training size.
assertions.reader_inference: Simulation on synthetic data only.

assertions.value: The authors report on the quantum correlation identification task that for sample sizes exceeding 180, the averaged test accuracy from coreset is almost higher than the best accuracy from random sampling, which used a maximum of 900 training samples.
quotes: for sample sizes exceeding 180, the averaged test accuracy obtained by coreset is almost higher than the best accuracy achieved by random sampling.
The red dash lines in subfigure (i) and (ii) denote the maximum test accuracy attained by the classifier through random sampling, with a maximum of 900 training samples.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The word 'almost' marks that the coreset is not higher at every size.

assertions.value: The authors state that their evidence is systematic numerical simulations on three tasks: synthetic data classification, identification of quantum correlations, and quantum compiling.
quotes: Through systematic numerical simulations, we illuminate the potential of coreset selection in expediting tasks encompassing synthetic data classification, identification of quantum correlations, and quantum compiling.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own evidence scope in the abstract.
assertions.reader_inference: No hardware run is reported in the sections read.

papers.title_in_file: Generative quantum advantage for classical and quantum problems
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, Sections II to IV (theory statements, experimental results, discussion) and figure captions. Appendices (formal proofs, device details) not read.
papers.what_it_is: A Google Quantum AI paper that defines generative quantum advantage and reports theory plus superconducting-processor experiments on learning and sampling hard-to-simulate quantum models.

assertions.value: The authors state, under standard complexity-theoretic conjectures, that there exist distributions mapping classical bit strings to bit strings that a quantum computer can efficiently learn to generate from classical data samples but that are hard to generate with classical computers.
quotes: Under standard complexity-theoretic conjectures, there exist distributions
that a quantum computer can efficiently learn to generate using classical data samples, but are hard to generate with classical computers.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 1 (informal), p.3; formal proof stated as Theorems 12 and 13 in Appendix H, not read. Conditional on complexity-theoretic conjectures.
assertions.reader_inference: The result is conditional and covers constructed distributions, not natural data.

assertions.value: The authors report that on a superconducting processor with up to 68 physical qubits, corresponding to an effective shallow dimension of 816 qubits, quantum models showed a considerable performance advantage over transformer and XGBoost classical models as size increased.
assertions.anchor: Section III, experiments on learning to generate bitstrings, p.7-8 (Fig. 2d)
quotes: we vary the physical qubits up to 68, corresponding to an effective shallow dimension of 816 qubits.
as size increases the quantum models demonstrate a considerable performance advantage over the classical models, both of which use classical learning algorithms here.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical hardware result from one study (Google authors), scored by cross-entropy benchmarking against selected classical models.
assertions.reader_inference: The classical comparators are generic sequence models. The authors note a tensor network approach may still sample these distributions at some sizes.

assertions.value: The authors state that 816 shallow qubits are not yet expected to be in the beyond-classical regime, and that a more efficient simulator, such as a tensor network-based approach, may still be able to sample from these distributions at some sizes.
quotes: Hence, 816 shallow qubits are not yet expected to be in the beyond-classical regime.
A more efficient quantum circuit simulator able to handle additional structure, such as a tensor network-based approach, may still be able to sample from these distributions at some sizes
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own limit of the 68-qubit experiment, Section III, p.8-9.
assertions.reader_inference: The hardware experiment itself is not a beyond-classical demonstration; that claim rests on the inferred mapping.

assertions.value: The authors state that an IDQNN representation of the beyond-classical limit is estimated to require 34,304 shallow qubits, mapped to deep circuits on 67 physical qubits, and that compared with the Frontier supercomputer at approximately 18,000 years of runtime the quantum model mapped to real hardware today exhibits a performance advantage.
quotes: an IDQNN representation of the beyond-classical limit is estimated to require 34,304 shallow qubits, mapped to deep circuits on 67 physical qubits.
Even compared to the Frontier supercomputer equipped with approximately 18,000 years of runtime, the quantum model mapped to real hardware today exhibits a performance advantage
assertions.certainty_reason: Result inferred by mapping published random-circuit-sampling data (Ref. 30) onto the model; not a direct run at that scale.
assertions.reader_inference: Authors are Google Quantum AI staff describing results on Google hardware. The estimate is an upper bound on resources by the authors' own statement and depends on the mapping.

papers.title_in_file: PALQO: Physics-informed Model for Accelerating Large-scale Quantum Optimization
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, method overview, main experiments (Section 4), conclusion and limitations, and the quantum machine learning experiment in Appendix F.2. Proof of the generalization result and other appendices not read.
papers.what_it_is: PALQO, a physics-informed neural network that predicts parameter updates of variational quantum algorithms on the classical side to cut quantum measurement cost, tested by numerical simulation up to 40 qubits.

assertions.value: The authors report from numerical experiments that PALQO achieves up to a 30x speedup compared to conventional methods and reduces quantum resource costs by as much as 90% for tasks involving up to 40 qubits, while maintaining competitive accuracy.
quotes: Through systematic numerical experiments, we demonstrate that our method achieves up to a 30x speedup compared to conventional methods and reduces quantum resource costs by as much as 90% for tasks involving up to 40 qubits
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result from one study; the figures are best cases.
assertions.reader_inference: The 30x and 90% figures are maxima. The paper itself reports a large variance in speedup.

assertions.value: The authors state that they conduct extensive numerical simulations on ground state preparation tasks (transverse-field Ising model, Heisenberg model, multiple molecule systems) with results up to 40 qubits, learning from a limited set of initial parameter updates obtained from quantum devices.
quotes: We then conduct extensive numerical simulations on different ground state preparation tasks
Simulation results up to 40 qubits indicate that by learning from a limited set of initial parameter updates obtained from quantum devices
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own evidence scope in Section 1, p.2.
assertions.reader_inference: No run on quantum hardware is reported in the sections read; the quantum-device data are themselves simulated.

assertions.value: The authors state that PALQO lowers the number of quantum queries compared to vanilla VQE but may diminish some quantum advantages, and that mitigating the high variance in speedup ratios is crucial for more stable and reliable performance.
quotes: While this lowers the number of quantum queries compared to vanilla VQE, it may diminish some quantum advantages.
mitigating the high variance in speedup ratios is crucial for achieving more stable and reliable performance.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own limits in Section 5.
assertions.reader_inference: Section 4 also says the speedup depends on the specific system configuration.

assertions.value: The authors report on a 4-qubit QNN classification task over the Iris dataset that PALQO reaches an average accuracy over 90% by the 120 steps, while the baseline model only achieves 75%.
quotes: We construct the 4-qubit QNN with 3-layer HEA
it reaches an average accuracy over 90% by the 120 steps, significantly outperforming the baseline model, which only achieves 75%.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result from one study on one small dataset (Iris).
assertions.reader_inference: This is the only machine learning workload read in the paper, and it is placed in the appendix.

papers.title_in_file: Towards Quantum Machine Learning with Tensor Networks
papers.what_it_is: A proposal for discriminative and generative quantum learning with tree and matrix product state tensor network circuits, with numerical experiments on MNIST digit pairs and a noise study.

assertions.value: The authors report that networks trained with their chosen hyper-parameters achieved an average test accuracy above 95% over classifiers for each of the 45 pairs of handwritten digits 0 through 9, using 64 pixel images.
quotes: we show results below for classifiers trained to distinguish between each of the 45 pairs of handwritten digits 0 through 9.
were able to achieve an average test accuracy above 95%.
the difficulty of distinguishing similar digits using 64 pixel images.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical numerical-simulation result from one study on a downsampled binary task.
assertions.reader_inference: The authors note significant differences across pairs and that hyper-parameters affect which pairs do best.

assertions.value: The authors report that under simulated amplitude damping and dephasing noise the typical change in test accuracy across all models was about 0.004, and the largest reduction was a model that dropped from a test accuracy of 0.88 to 0.806.
assertions.anchor: Section IV.C, Noise Resilience, p.12 (Figs. 13 and 14)
quotes: The typical change in test accuracy across all of the models due to the noise was about 0.004.
which dropped from a test accuracy of 0.88 to 0.806.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical numerical-simulation result from one study with an assumed noise model.
assertions.reader_inference: The noise model has only amplitude damping and dephasing in the contraction step; the paper says a different set of hyper-parameters was needed to train under noise.

assertions.value: The authors state that tensor network circuits can provide qubit-efficient schemes where, depending on the architecture, the number of physical qubits required scales only logarithmically with, or independently of, the input or output data sizes.
quotes: Tensor network circuits can also provide qubitefficient schemes where, depending on the architecture, the number of physical qubits required scales only logarithmically with, or independently of the input or output data sizes.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the scaling of its own proposed circuit designs in the abstract and Section IV.
assertions.reader_inference: This is a resource-count property of the proposed circuits, not a performance result; it requires hardware that can measure single qubits without disturbing the others.

assertions.value: The authors state that they performed some simple numerical experiments showing the algorithms can tolerate a high level of noise, and that additional empirical demonstrations and a theoretical explanation of how generic this property is would be very useful.
quotes: We performed some simple numerical experiments to show that these algorithms can tolerate a high level of noise, but additional empirical demonstrations as well as a theoretical explanation of how generic this property is would be very useful.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own limit in the closing discussion.
